title: Elara’s Orchard: Blight and Branching Choices

scenario.title: Elara’s Orchard: Blight and Branching Choices
scenario.setting: Elara’s Orchard is divided into 12 interconnected microcells: heirloom apple guild beds, mason bee nesting boxes, rain-harvest cisterns, and stone fruit barrier rows. Planted by their great-grandmother 13 years prior, it’s now sustained by three sibling stewards and a rotating crew of local volunteers, having cleared its first critical growth year and entered its second decade of production. The core dilemma hinges on the orchard’s original cider apple tree, whose root flare shows signs of neonatal blight, splitting the siblings over how best to save it.

characters.name: Mara
characters.tendencies: She curates the siblings' shared digital archive of great-grandma's orchard notes, cross-referencing weekly microcell surveys against Elara’s original planting plan. She refuses to consider untested treatments because she fears losing the orchard's original ancestral lineage.

characters.name: Lila
characters.tendencies: She’s spent the last three months trialing organic copper sulfate sprays on the affected tree, refining application rates to minimize harm to nearby pollinator habitats. She argues that delaying the experimental treatment will lead to the tree's death before the autumn harvest.

characters.name: Javi
characters.tendencies: He runs the orchard’s community-supported agriculture program, hosting monthly open houses and recruiting local volunteers to assist with daily maintenance. He worries that diverting all their resources to saving one tree will leave other parts of the orchard’s microcell network under-cared for.

characters.name: Kaelin
characters.tendencies: They’re a local teen volunteer who first discovered the orchard through Javi’s social media posts, and they’ve begun documenting the orchard’s unplanned volunteer saplings. They’ve noticed new shoots sprouting from the base of the blighted tree, and they advocate for letting natural regeneration lead the way.

turns.name: DM
turns.text: Fog rolls off the cistern row as the tide-bell tolls terce, and three of you stand at the base of the original cider apple — Mara kneeling at the weeping root flare, Lila clutching the copper pruning shears she's already sharpened twice, Javi hauling the last rain-barrel down from the heirloom guild beds because something has fouled the cistern water overnight with a faint sour reek. The neonatal blight is spreading faster than any text in Elara's journals promised, and Kaelin is still unaccounted for out at the mason bee boxes where the buzzing has gone strangely silent. Within the hour you must decide whether Lila cuts the infected flare wood tonight before the fog-borne spores ride the next tide-wind into the stone fruit barrier, or whether Mara's slow seaweed-and-ash packing buys the old tree time at the risk of everything planted since. Javi waits at the cistern valve, hands on the release that would flood the root cell with fresh rainwater — do you open it, or do you send someone running for Kaelin first?

turns.name: Mara
turns.text:
I just cross-referenced this week’s microcell survey against Great-Grandma’s original orchard blueprint. This weeping root flare has mild signs of nutrient stress, but the surrounding clover and comfrey guild matches her exact planting notes, so we can’t risk untested foliar sprays or unapproved pruning with those shears that might disrupt the ancestral ecosystem. We should test the adjacent cistern’s water pH first to rule out nutrient uptake issues before we consider any further steps.
[keeps one palm pressed lightly to the root flare to monitor soil moisture while gesturing toward the cistern row with her other hand]

turns.name: Javi
turns.text:
I hate to be the downer here, but our open volunteer slots for the mason bee nesting box repairs and cistern filter swaps are nearly all gone for the rest of the month. We can’t pour every spare minute into this old apple tree without leaving half the orchard’s microcells unmaintained.
[folds the crumpled volunteer scheduling sheet in his hands and nods toward the distant row of rain cisterns]

turns.name: Kaelin
turns.text:
Lila, put those copper pruners down for a minute— I’ve been documenting all the orchard’s volunteer saplings, and these fuzzy new shoots at the blighted tree’s base are its natural offspring, not invasive weeds. Let’s skip pruning this spot so they can grow on their own, yeah?
[kneels at the root flare to brush away a layer of damp leaf litter to better show the cluster of tender saplings]

turns.name: Mara
turns.text:
I already logged both the shrinking volunteer slots and this tree’s natural sapling shoots in my cross-referenced microcell survey notes last night. We should pull the seasonal steward contact list from the shared archive instead of scrambling for impromptu help, and stick strictly to great-grandma’s recorded comfrey tea treatment for the root stress to protect the orchard’s original ancestral lineage.
[tucks a small clump of the adjacent comfrey around the tree’s root flare before tapping her weathered archival tablet to pull up the historical steward roster]

turns.name: Lila
turns.text: "Lila": "Those 'offspring' are suckering off the same compromised root system, Kaelin—if the mother tree goes, they inherit the blight along with the roots. My trials cut the application rate to a tenth of standard and I've logged zero pollinator kills across three spray

turns.name: Javi
turns.text:
I lean in to get a clear look at the fuzzy sapling shoots Kaelin documented, nodding along with the good news. Even with this natural backup for the original tree, we can’t ignore our dwindling volunteer slots for the mason bee repairs and cistern filter swaps — those tasks keep the whole orchard’s microcells running smoothly.
[tucks Mara’s loose survey sheet into her arm wrap before grabbing his weathered orchard clipboard to jot a quick reminder]

turns.name: Kaelin
turns.text:
"Wait, hold on, I wasn’t done earlier—these fuzzy new shoots aren’t invasive weeds, they’re the blighted cider tree’s own natural regrowth. I’ve been documenting every volunteer sapling across the microcells for weeks, and letting these grow would let the orchard repopulate on its own without extra, unnecessary work."
[pulls a weatherproof field notebook from their canvas cargo pocket to jot a quick note beside the root flare]

dm_closing: The comfrey is tucked at the root flare and Mara's tablet hums as the historical steward roster finally surfaces—names, tides, and treatment records all in one place, so the group parts with a plan: no impromptu recruits, no off-book sprays, just great-grandma's recorded tea until the root stress is read again. What carries over is the unresolved split over Kaelin
